name: India

laws.title: Digital Personal Data Protection Rules, 2025
laws.citation: G.S.R. 846(E), 13 Nov 2025; commencement of the Act by G.S.R. 843(E)

laws.title: Information Technology Act, 2000 — s. 43A and the SPDI Rules, 2011 (interim regime)
laws.citation: IT Act s. 43A; IT (Reasonable Security Practices and Procedures and Sensitive Personal Data or Information) Rules, 2011 — s. 43A omitted by DPDP Act s. 44(2) on its commencement

regulators.name: Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY)

scopeNotes: The DPDP Act commences in phases under G.S.R. 843(E) of 13 Nov 2025 (Gazette published 13/14 Nov 2025): Board and procedural provisions immediately; Consent Manager provisions after one year (Nov 2026); and the core Data Fiduciary obligations (ss. 3–5, 6 except (9), 7–17, penalties in ss. 27–34 and the omission of IT Act s. 43A by s. 44(2)) after eighteen months, i.e. on or about 13–14 May 2027. Until then the IT Act s. 43A / SPDI Rules regime continues. The Act applies to digital personal data processed in India and to processing outside India connected with offering goods or services to people in India. It has no general legitimate-interests ground but lists 'legitimate uses', including employment purposes. Cross-border transfers are permitted except to countries the Government restricts by notification. Obligation dates below assume 13 May 2027; confirm the exact day with counsel.

obligations.title: Prepare the Indian entity for DPDP commencement (May 2027)
obligations.requirement: The core DPDP obligations apply from eighteen months after publication of the 13 November 2025 notification (on or about 13–14 May 2027). The GDPR programme covers much of the substance, but India-specific items — stand-alone itemised notices, breach reporting to the Board for every breach, 1-year log retention, 90-day grievance handling and published contact details — must be built in time. Penalties reach INR 250 crore for security failures.
obligations.appliesIfNote: Applies because the group has an Indian entity processing digital personal data.
actionSteps: Run a DPDP gap assessment of the Indian entity against the GDPR baseline.
Plan remediation to complete before May 2027.
Monitor Government notifications (restricted transfer countries, Significant Data Fiduciary designations).
obligations.deadlineOrTimeline: Core obligations from on or about 13 May 2027
obligations.penaltyNote: Up to INR 250 crore (security safeguards); up to INR 200 crore (breach notification; children); up to INR 50 crore (other violations).

obligations.title: Until May 2027, comply with the IT Act s. 43A / SPDI Rules regime
obligations.requirement: Until DPDP s. 44(2) commences and omits IT Act s. 43A, bodies corporate handling sensitive personal data or information remain subject to the reasonable-security-practices regime of s. 43A and the SPDI Rules 2011 (privacy policy, consent for sensitive data, transfer conditions, grievance officer). The SPDI Rules text was not retrieved in this research pass.
obligations.appliesIfNote: Applies until May 2027 because the Indian entity handles sensitive data (health, biometrics, financial).
actionSteps: Ask Indian counsel to confirm current SPDI compliance for the Indian entity pending DPDP commencement.

sources.pinpoint: DPDP Act s. 44(2)(a) (omits IT Act s. 43A on commencement)

obligations.title: Base processing on consent or a listed legitimate use (incl. employment)
obligations.requirement: Personal data may be processed only with consent or for a 'legitimate use' listed in s. 7, which includes processing for purposes of employment or to safeguard the employer from loss or liability (e.g. preventing corporate espionage, protecting trade secrets and IP, or providing a service or benefit sought by an employee). There is no general legitimate-interests ground, so B2B marketing, CRM and analytics generally need consent.
obligations.appliesIfNote: Applies to every Data Fiduciary processing digital personal data in India.
actionSteps: Map Indian processing to consent or a s. 7 legitimate use; HR processing can generally rely on s. 7(i).
Implement consent (with easy withdrawal) for non-employment processing currently on GDPR legitimate interests.

obligations.title: Give stand-alone, itemised consent notices with a withdrawal link
obligations.requirement: Consent notices must be understandable on their own, give in clear language an itemised description of the personal data and the specified purposes and goods/services or uses enabled, and provide a link and other means to withdraw consent (as easily as it was given), exercise rights and complain to the Board.
obligations.appliesIfNote: Applies wherever the Indian entity relies on consent.
actionSteps: Create India-specific stand-alone notices with itemised data lists for each consent-based activity.

obligations.title: Implement minimum security safeguards and keep access logs for one year
obligations.requirement: Data Fiduciaries must protect personal data (including at processors) with reasonable safeguards including, at a minimum: encryption/masking/tokenisation; access controls; logging and monitoring to detect and investigate unauthorised access; continuity measures such as backups; retention of logs and data for one year for detection and remediation; contractual safeguards with processors; and organisational measures.
obligations.appliesIfNote: Applies to every Data Fiduciary processing digital personal data in India.
actionSteps: Map the group ISMS to Rule 6 minimums.
Set log retention for Indian systems to at least one year.
Flow Rule 6 requirements into processor contracts.
obligations.penaltyNote: Failure to take reasonable security safeguards: up to INR 250 crore.

obligations.title: Report every personal data breach to the Board (detailed report within 72 hours) and to individuals
obligations.requirement: On becoming aware of any personal data breach — there is no risk threshold — the Data Fiduciary must inform each affected Data Principal without delay (nature, consequences, mitigation, safety steps, contact) and inform the Data Protection Board without delay, followed within 72 hours (or longer if the Board allows) by a detailed report on facts, causes, mitigation, findings about the responsible person and remedial measures.
obligations.appliesIfNote: Applies to every Data Fiduciary processing digital personal data in India.
actionSteps: Add an India track to the group incident procedure: notify the Board of all breaches, not only risky ones.
obligations.deadlineOrTimeline: Without delay; detailed Board report within 72 hours
obligations.penaltyNote: Failure to notify the Board or affected individuals: up to INR 200 crore.

obligations.title: Retain processing logs for at least one year, then erase
obligations.requirement: Data Fiduciaries must retain personal data, associated traffic data and logs of processing for at least one year from the processing for the purposes in the Seventh Schedule, then erase them unless other law requires retention. Certain classes of fiduciaries listed in the Third Schedule must also erase data after inactivity periods with 48 hours' prior notice.
obligations.appliesIfNote: Applies to every Data Fiduciary processing digital personal data in India.
actionSteps: Update the retention schedule for India: minimum one-year log retention, followed by erasure.

obligations.title: Publish a contact person for data questions (India-based DPO if Significant)
obligations.requirement: Every Data Fiduciary must prominently publish on its website or app, and include in every rights response, the business contact of its Data Protection Officer (if applicable) or a person able to answer questions about processing. Significant Data Fiduciaries must appoint a DPO based in India who is responsible to the Board of Directors.
obligations.appliesIfNote: Applies to every Data Fiduciary processing digital personal data in India.
actionSteps: Name an India contact for data questions and publish it on the Indian website.
If the entity is notified as a Significant Data Fiduciary, appoint an India-based DPO.

obligations.title: Publish how to exercise rights and resolve grievances within 90 days
obligations.requirement: Data Fiduciaries must publish the means and identifiers needed to exercise rights (access to information, correction, completion, updating, erasure, nomination) and a grievance redressal period not exceeding 90 days, with measures to meet it.
obligations.appliesIfNote: Applies to every Data Fiduciary processing digital personal data in India.
actionSteps: Add India to the DSAR tool with a published grievance SLA (≤ 90 days; aim for the group's 30-day standard).

obligations.title: Check transfers against Government restrictions (negative-list model)
obligations.requirement: Personal data may be transferred outside India except to countries the Central Government restricts by notification, and subject to any requirements the Government specifies about making data available to foreign States or entities under their control. Sectoral laws imposing stricter localisation still apply, and Significant Data Fiduciaries may be required to keep specified data in India.
obligations.appliesIfNote: Applies because Indian personal data is transferred to or accessed from abroad.
actionSteps: Monitor Government notifications under s. 16(1) and Rule 15.
Confirm no sectoral localisation rule covers the entity's data.

obligations.title: Obtain verifiable parental consent before processing children's data
obligations.requirement: Before processing any personal data of a child (under 18), the Data Fiduciary must obtain verifiable parental consent, with due diligence that the parent is an identifiable adult, using reliable identity/age details or a virtual token from an authorised entity.
obligations.appliesIfNote: Applies because you process personal data of children in India.
actionSteps: Implement age-gating and a verifiable parental-consent flow for any child-facing processing.
obligations.penaltyNote: Violations of obligations relating to children: up to INR 200 crore.

upcomingChanges.title: Consent Manager provisions commence
upcomingChanges.summary: DPDP Act s. 6(9) and Rule 4 (Consent Managers) come into force one year after Gazette publication of 13/14 Nov 2025.

upcomingChanges.title: Core DPDP obligations commence; IT Act s. 43A omitted
upcomingChanges.summary: Eighteen months after publication: Data Fiduciary obligations (ss. 3–17), penalties and s. 44(2) (omission of IT Act s. 43A) take effect, with DPDP Rules 3, 5–16, 22 and 23.
